title: After a star flared in 2002, its echo of light seemed to spread faster than light

cover.alt: A glowing shell of red and brown dust with swirls and eddies, surrounding a bright red star among blue-white stars, photographed by Hubble.

body: In early 2002 the star **V838 Monocerotis**, about 19,000 light-years away, suddenly brightened to hundreds of thousands of times the Sun’s luminosity. Its flash lit up clouds of dust around it, and light that bounced off the dust took a longer path to us than light that came straight. So for years afterwards we saw the flash reach dust further and further from the star: a growing light echo. The rings seem to spread faster than light, but nothing is moving that fast; we are seeing different parts of the cloud light up in turn.

slides.alt: Blended sequence of Hubble images: a small glowing ring around a red star swells into a huge shell of swirling red and brown dust that fills the frame.
slides.caption: Eight Hubble images of V838 Monocerotis, taken over the years after its 2002 outburst, blended into one sped-up sequence: the echo sweeps outward through the dust.

slides.prompt: What made V838 Monocerotis flare up?
slides.detail: Outbursts like this one, called luminous red novae, are thought to be caused by stellar mergers, but the reason for this one is still uncertain.

slides.question: Why does the light echo seem to spread faster than light?
options: Dust further out is lit later
The blast pushed the dust outward
slides.explanation: The dust isn’t moving. Light reflected from dust further from the star travels a longer route, so that dust appears to light up later.
